common_name: Mattamuskeet Apple (Coastal North Carolina Heirloom Winter Keeper)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mattamuskeet originated as a seedling near Lake Mattamuskeet in Hyde County on North Carolina's low-lying coastal plain, so it tolerates the humid, mild-winter conditions of the lower South better than many mountain-bred heirlooms, and it needs a second apple cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Mattamuskeet carries an old legend that its first seed was recovered from the gizzard of a wild goose by Mattamuskeet Indians living beside the lake that gives the apple its name. The medium to large fruit is roundish to oblate and slightly conical, with tough skin mostly covered in dull purplish or rusty red over a yellow ground color, and firm, pale yellow flesh that is only moderately juicy and somewhat sharp at harvest but turns sweeter, more aromatic, and spicier after a few weeks in storage. It ripens very late, often not until October or November, and keeps for months without any chilling requirement, reaching peak flavor as late as the following spring. Because it comes from North Carolina's warm, humid coastal plain rather than the Appalachian uplands, Mattamuskeet has a comparatively low chill-hour need and is one of the more Gulf Coast-friendly Southern winter keepers, prized locally as a close hot-climate substitute for Virginia Winesap.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples

common_name: Terry Winter Apple (Antebellum Georgia Heirloom Keeper)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; Terry Winter originated before the Civil War on a farm in Fulton County, Georgia, and its Deep South origin gives it a lower chill requirement than most Appalachian-bred keeper apples, though it still needs a second apple cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Terry Winter was first grafted and sold by a local Georgia nurseryman in 1868 from a tree on the farm of a Mr. Terry near present-day Atlanta, and by the 1880s it had spread from Georgia into neighboring Southern states as a dependable late keeper. Fruit is medium or smaller, roundish, flattened at the ends, with thick, tough skin covered in dull strawberry red broken by faint stripes and a heavy gray bloom, over numerous whitish-and-russet dots. The almost-white flesh is fine-grained, crisp, and juicy with a mild subacid flavor, ripening in October to November and storing exceptionally well into winter. As a Deep South heirloom bred for Georgia's warm climate, it fills the same late-keeper niche as Northern winter apples but with a chill requirement well suited to Gulf South orchards.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples
NC Historic Sites — Horne Creek Farm Southern Heritage Apple Orchard, Apple Index

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Dayton carries field immunity to apple scab from the Vf gene, which cuts back on fungicide sprays in the humid, disease-prone South, and it needs a second apple cultivar nearby since it is not self-fruitful.

directions: Dayton was released in 1987 by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistant apple breeding program and named in honor of Daniel F. Dayton, longtime leader of the University of Illinois arm of that program. The vigorous, upright tree sets a moderate annual crop of large, glossy red apples with good, full-flavored dessert quality, ripening in the first week of September. Its Vf-gene scab immunity has held up through more than a decade of field testing across Illinois, Indiana, New Jersey, Oregon, and several Canadian and European research stations, making it one of the more reliable low-spray choices for humid Southern growing conditions. It pairs well with other early to midseason disease-resistant cultivars such as Williams' Pride or Pristine for extended early harvest.
sources: ISHS Acta Horticulturae — History of the PRI Apple Breeding Program
PRI Disease Resistant Apple Breeding Program (Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois)
Cornell University — Apple Scab Susceptibility of Common Cultivars

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Prima's Vf-gene scab resistance reduces the fungicide program needed in the warm, humid Southern growing season, and it needs a second apple cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Released in 1970, Prima was the first apple cultivar to come out of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistant apple breeding program and the first widely distributed scab-immune apple in North America, opening the door for the later Priscilla, Jonafree, Redfree, Dayton, Williams' Pride, Enterprise, GoldRush, and Pristine releases from the same program. The medium-sized fruit has red-striped skin over a yellow ground color and crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh, ripening in late summer to early fall for an early-season harvest. Because it carries field immunity to apple scab, Prima needs far fewer fungicide applications than old standard cultivars, a real advantage in the humid Gulf South where scab and other fungal diseases pressure apple trees hardest. It remains a useful historical and practical choice for low-spray orchards looking for an early disease-resistant apple.
sources: ISHS Acta Horticulturae — History of the PRI Apple Breeding Program
PRI Disease Resistant Apple Breeding Program (Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois)
